model-expansion-d31b2ee9.title: Effective Lagrangian for Physics Beyond the Standard Model

\\mathcal{L}_{BSM}.name: Beyond-Standard-Model Lagrangian Density
\\mathcal{L}_{BSM}.description: The effective Lagrangian density describing both Standard Model physics and the low-energy effects of new physics.

\\mathcal{L}_{SM}.name: Standard Model Lagrangian Density
\\mathcal{L}_{SM}.description: The Lagrangian density for the Standard Model of particle physics, containing all known fundamental particles and their interactions.

c_i.name: Wilson Coefficient
c_i.description: A dimensionless coupling constant that parameterizes the strength of the interaction corresponding to the operator $\mathcal{O}_i$.

\\Lambda.name: Cutoff Scale
\\Lambda.description: The high-energy scale at which new physics becomes manifest and the effective field theory description breaks down. Often associated with the mass of new, heavy particles.

d.name: Suppression Exponent
d.description: An integer exponent related to the mass dimension of the operator $\mathcal{O}_i$, typically $d = (\text{dim}(\mathcal{O}_i)) - 4$. For dimension-5 operators, $d=1$; for dimension-6, $d=2$.

\\mathcal{O}_i.name: Higher-Dimensional Operator
\\mathcal{O}_i.description: An operator constructed from Standard Model fields, invariant under SM gauge symmetries, with a mass dimension $d_{op} > 4$.

\\sum.name: Summation
\\sum.description: A summation over all possible higher-dimensional operators allowed by the symmetries of the theory.

model-expansion-d31b2ee9.interpretation: The equation $\mathcal{L}_{BSM} = \mathcal{L}_{SM} + \sum \frac{c_i}{\Lambda^d} \mathcal{O}_i$ defines the Lagrangian for a system that includes physics Beyond the Standard Model ($\mathcal{L}_{BSM}$). It begins with the complete, renormalizable Lagrangian of the Standard Model, $\mathcal{L}_{SM}$. To this, it adds a sum of correction terms representing new, unobserved phenomena. Each term consists of an operator $\mathcal{O}_i$, which is a combination of Standard Model fields with a mass dimension greater than 4. The strength of each new interaction is governed by a corresponding dimensionless 'Wilson coefficient' $c_i$. These terms are suppressed by powers of a large energy scale $\Lambda$, which represents the 'cutoff' of the effective theory—the scale at which the new particles or interactions would become directly observable. The exponent $d$ is a positive integer, typically related to the mass dimension of the operator $\mathcal{O}_i$ (denoted $d_{op}$) via $d = d_{op} - 4$. For example, the leading BSM contributions often come from dimension-6 operators ($d_{op}=6$), for which the suppression factor is $\Lambda^{2}$. In the low-energy limit where experimental energies $E \ll \Lambda$, terms with higher dimension are increasingly suppressed, and $\mathcal{L}_{SM}$ provides an excellent approximation of reality.
model-expansion-d31b2ee9.symmetry_origin: The structure of this Lagrangian is constrained by the principle of locality and the gauge symmetries of the Standard Model, $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$. The Standard Model Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{SM}$ is the most general renormalizable Lagrangian invariant under this gauge group. The higher-dimensional operators $\mathcal{O}_i$ are also constructed to be invariant under this same gauge symmetry, ensuring that the low-energy predictions of the theory respect these fundamental symmetries observed in nature.
model-expansion-d31b2ee9.limits_and_boundary: In the limit that the new physics scale becomes infinitely large, $\Lambda \to \infty$, all correction terms vanish ($\frac{c_i}{\Lambda^d} \to 0$). The Lagrangian thus reduces to the Standard Model Lagrangian, $\mathcal{L}_{BSM} \to \mathcal{L}_{SM}$. This is known as the decoupling limit. Conversely, the expansion is only valid for processes with characteristic energy scales $E$ much less than the cutoff, $E \ll \Lambda$. As $E \to \Lambda$, the effective field theory breaks down, as all operators in the infinite sum become equally important, and a complete, 'UV-complete' theory of the underlying physics is required.
model-expansion-d31b2ee9.conceptual_definition: In the framework of effective field theory (EFT), the effects of unknown high-energy physics at a scale $\Lambda$ can be systematically parameterized at lower energies. The Lagrangian for physics Beyond the Standard Model, $\mathcal{L}_{BSM}$, is constructed by adding a tower of non-renormalizable, higher-dimensional operators $\mathcal{O}_i$ to the renormalizable Standard Model Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{SM}$. Each operator $\mathcal{O}_i$ is constructed from Standard Model fields, respects the SM gauge symmetries, and has a mass dimension greater than four. The effects of these operators are suppressed by powers of the high-energy scale $\Lambda$.
model-expansion-d31b2ee9.intuitive_summary: Imagine the Standard Model is a very detailed, accurate map of a city. This formula acts as a guide for describing the subtle, long-range effects of unseen, distant mountains on the city's environment. We don't know the exact shape of the mountains (the operators $\mathcal{O}_i$), but we can parameterize their influence via coefficients ($c_i$) and know that their effects are weaker the farther away they are (the high-energy scale $\Lambda$).
model-expansion-d31b2ee9.description: This formula represents the Lagrangian for physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) as an effective field theory. It extends the Standard Model Lagrangian with a sum of higher-dimensional operators, suppressed by a high-energy scale $\Lambda$.

conserved-ratio-1d09af87.title: Baryon-to-Entropy Ratio

Y_B.name: Baryon-to-Entropy Ratio
Y_B.description: The conserved ratio of net baryon number density to entropy density.

n_B.name: Baryon Number Density
n_B.description: The number of baryons per unit volume.

n_{\\bar{B}}.name: Antibaryon Number Density
n_{\\bar{B}}.description: The number of antibaryons per unit volume.

s.name: Entropy Density
s.description: The total entropy per unit volume of the cosmic fluid, in natural units where Boltzmann's constant $k_B=1$.

\\eta.name: Baryon-to-Photon Ratio
\\eta.description: The ratio of the net baryon number density to the photon number density.

conserved-ratio-1d09af87.interpretation: The formula consists of a definition and a cosmologically important approximation. The definition part, $Y_B = (n_B - n_{\bar{B}})/s$, establishes the ratio, where $Y_B$ is the dimensionless baryon-to-entropy ratio, $n_B$ is the number density of baryons, $n_{\bar{B}}$ is the number density of antibaryons, and $s$ is the total entropy density of the cosmic fluid. The term $n_B - n_{\bar{B}}$ represents the net baryon asymmetry. The approximation, $Y_B \approx \eta / 7.04$, connects $Y_B$ to the baryon-to-photon ratio, $\eta = (n_B - n_{\bar{B}})/n_\gamma$, where $n_\gamma$ is the photon number density. The numerical factor $7.04$ is derived from the statistical mechanics of the Standard Model particle content after electron-positron annihilation, where the total entropy density is related to the photon number density by $s \approx 7.04 k_B n_\gamma$. In natural units ($k_B=1$), this becomes $s \approx 7.04 n_\gamma$, leading directly to the approximation.
conserved-ratio-1d09af87.symmetry_origin: The conservation of the numerator, the net baryon number $N_B - N_{\bar{B}}$ in a comoving volume, stems from the (approximate) global $U(1)_B$ symmetry of the Standard Model. The conservation of the denominator, the total entropy $S = sV$ in a comoving volume $V$, is a consequence of the Second Law of Thermodynamics applied to the universe undergoing adiabatic expansion in thermal equilibrium.
conserved-ratio-1d09af87.limits_and_boundary: In a hypothetical early universe with perfect matter-antimatter symmetry before baryogenesis, $n_B = n_{\bar{B}}$, which would imply $Y_B = 0$. The non-zero value observed today is a direct consequence of baryogenesis. The approximation $Y_B \approx \eta/7.04$ is specifically valid for the epoch after electron-positron annihilation ($T \ll m_e c^2$) and assumes no significant entropy production has occurred since that time. If other relativistic species were present or if there were significant out-of-equilibrium processes, the factor $7.04$ would change.
conserved-ratio-1d09af87.conceptual_definition: The baryon-to-entropy ratio, denoted $Y_B$, is defined as the net baryon number density, $n_B - n_{ ar{B}}$, divided by the total entropy density, $s$. This ratio is a fundamental conserved quantity in an adiabatically expanding universe after the epoch of baryogenesis, making it a more robust invariant than the baryon-to-photon ratio $\eta$.
conserved-ratio-1d09af87.intuitive_summary: Imagine a fixed chunk of the expanding universe. While particles and photons are created or annihilated, the total entropy in this chunk remains constant. The baryon-to-entropy ratio $Y_B$ is like a cosmic 'serial number' stamped on this chunk, telling us the permanent surplus of matter particles (baryons) per unit of this conserved entropy. This number was fixed in the first moments of the universe and hasn't changed since.
conserved-ratio-1d09af87.description: Defines the baryon-to-entropy ratio, a key conserved quantity in cosmology that relates the net baryon number density to the total entropy density, and provides its approximate relation to the baryon-to-photon ratio.

human-filter-cf7ccc8d.title: Distinction between Formal Reason and Physical Intuition

\\text{Reason}.name: Formal Reason
\\text{Reason}.description: Represents the formal, logical-mathematical, and empirically validated framework of physics.

\\text{Intuition}.name: Physical Intuition
\\text{Intuition}.description: Represents subjective, common-sense expectations about physical phenomena, typically derived from macroscopic experience.

\\neq.name: Inequality Operator
\\neq.description: Asserts that the two conceptual frameworks, Reason and Intuition, are fundamentally distinct and often yield contradictory conclusions.

human-filter-cf7ccc8d.interpretation: The formula $\text{Reason} \neq \text{Intuition}$ is a conceptual inequality central to the epistemology of modern physics. The term $\text{Reason}$ symbolizes the rigorous framework of theoretical physics, built upon mathematical consistency, logical deduction, and experimental verification. The term $\text{Intuition}$ represents the set of a priori beliefs and cognitive shortcuts developed from interacting with the classical, macroscopic world. The inequality $\neq$ signifies that these two modes of cognition are not only different but often lead to contradictory conclusions, as seen in quantum mechanics (e.g., superposition, entanglement) and relativity (e.g., time dilation, length contraction). The parenthetical note, $(\text{Transcendental distinction})$, alludes to Kantian philosophy, suggesting that the structure of our innate intuition is insufficient to grasp the 'thing-in-itself' (noumenal reality), which can only be approached through the abstract structures of formal reason.
human-filter-cf7ccc8d.symmetry_origin: Not applicable; this is an epistemological principle concerning the cognitive frameworks used to understand physical laws, rather than a physical law derived from a symmetry.
human-filter-cf7ccc8d.limits_and_boundary: The distinction becomes most pronounced in regimes far from everyday experience. In the classical limit where $\hbar \to 0$ and velocities are much less than the speed of light ($v \ll c$), intuition often aligns with physical laws (e.g., Newtonian mechanics). However, in the quantum realm ($\hbar \neq 0$) or the relativistic realm ($v \to c$), intuition fails, and the inequality $\text{Reason} \neq \text{Intuition}$ becomes a critical guiding principle for physicists.
human-filter-cf7ccc8d.conceptual_definition: This principle posits a fundamental inequality, $\text{Reason} \neq \text{Intuition}$, where 'Reason' ($\text{Reason}$) represents the logical, mathematical, and empirically validated framework of physics, and 'Intuition' ($\text{Intuition}$) represents the subjective, often misleading, expectations derived from everyday sensory experience. The distinction is transcendental, implying that to grasp physical reality, one must transcend the limitations of naive perception.
human-filter-cf7ccc8d.intuitive_summary: Our gut feelings about how the world works, shaped by throwing balls and watching things fall, often fail spectacularly when we look at the very small (quantum mechanics) or the very fast (relativity). True physical understanding requires trusting the math and experiments, not our everyday common sense.
human-filter-cf7ccc8d.description: A foundational principle in the philosophy of physics asserting that formal, mathematical reasoning provides a description of reality that is fundamentally distinct from, and often contradictory to, subjective human intuition derived from macroscopic experience.

reactive-push-25b9cd08.title: Relativistic Rocket Equation (Velocity Form)

\\Delta v_{rel}.name: Change in Relative Velocity
\\Delta v_{rel}.description: The change in the rocket's velocity as measured in its initial inertial reference frame.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: The universal speed limit and propagation speed of electromagnetic fields in a vacuum.

\\tanh.name: Hyperbolic Tangent
\\tanh.description: A mathematical function that maps rapidity to a velocity factor, ensuring the result is bounded between -1 and 1.

v_e.name: Effective Exhaust Velocity
v_e.description: The velocity of the expelled mass relative to the rocket.

\\ln.name: Natural Logarithm
\\ln.description: The logarithm to the base e, used to relate the mass ratio to the change in velocity/rapidity.

m_0.name: Initial Mass
m_0.description: The total initial mass of the rocket, including fuel and payload.

m_f.name: Final Mass
m_f.description: The total final mass of the rocket after the propellant has been expended.

reactive-push-25b9cd08.interpretation: The formula $\Delta v_{rel} = c \tanh \left( \frac{v_e}{c} \ln \frac{m_0}{m_f} \right)$ quantifies the change in velocity, $\Delta v_{rel}$, in the rocket's initial reference frame. The term $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, a fundamental constant that acts as the upper limit to speed. The hyperbolic tangent function, $\tanh$, modulates the result, ensuring that the relative velocity change approaches but never exceeds $c$. The argument of the $\tanh$ function, $\frac{v_e}{c} \ln \frac{m_0}{m_f}$, is the change in rapidity, $\Delta \eta$. This dimensionless quantity contains the key parameters governing the rocket's performance: $v_e$ represents the effective exhaust velocity of the propellant relative to the rocket, and the ratio $v_e/c$ normalizes this velocity. The term $\ln(m_0/m_f)$ is the natural logarithm of the mass ratio, where $m_0$ is the initial total mass and $m_f$ is the final mass after propellant expulsion. This logarithmic term signifies that equal fractional changes in mass yield equal changes in rapidity.
reactive-push-25b9cd08.symmetry_origin: The equation is a direct consequence of the conservation of four-momentum in the absence of external forces, a principle derived from spacetime translational invariance via Noether's theorem. Its specific form, involving the hyperbolic tangent, arises from the structure of Lorentz transformations, which preserve the Minkowski spacetime interval and govern the composition of velocities in special relativity.
reactive-push-25b9cd08.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit where the exhaust velocity $v_e \ll c$, the argument of the hyperbolic tangent is small. Using the approximation $\tanh(x) \approx x$ for small $x$, the equation simplifies to $\Delta v_{rel} \approx c \left( \frac{v_e}{c} \ln \frac{m_0}{m_f} \right) = v_e \ln \frac{m_0}{m_f}$, which is the classical Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation. In the ultra-relativistic limit, as the mass ratio $m_0/m_f \to \infty$, the argument of the $\tanh$ function approaches infinity. Since $\lim_{x\to\infty} \tanh(x) = 1$, the velocity change $\Delta v_{rel}$ asymptotically approaches $c$. This demonstrates that the speed of light is an insurmountable barrier for a massive rocket.
reactive-push-25b9cd08.conceptual_definition: The change in velocity, $\Delta v_{rel}$, of a rocket in its initial rest frame is given by the speed of light, $c$, multiplied by the hyperbolic tangent of the change in rapidity, $\Delta \eta$. The rapidity change itself is the product of the normalized exhaust velocity, $v_e/c$, and the natural logarithm of the mass ratio, $\ln(m_0/m_f)$. This formulation is essential for scenarios where velocities are a significant fraction of the speed of light.
reactive-push-25b9cd08.intuitive_summary: Imagine the classic rocket equation that tells you how much faster you go by burning fuel. Now, add a universal speed limit: the speed of light. This formula is the result. The hyperbolic tangent function, $\tanh$, acts as a 'relativistic governor', ensuring that no matter how powerful your engine ($v_e$) or how much fuel you burn ($m_0/m_f$), your final speed will only get closer and closer to light speed, but never reach it.
reactive-push-25b9cd08.description: This equation provides the final velocity of a single-stage rocket, accounting for the principles of special relativity. It correctly models the velocity change by ensuring it asymptotically approaches, but never exceeds, the speed of light.

construction-energy-67a19021.title: Electrostatic Potential Energy of a Discrete Charge Distribution

U.name: Total Electrostatic Potential Energy
U.description: The total potential energy stored in the configuration of point charges, equivalent to the work done to assemble it.

\\sum.name: Summation Operator
\\sum.description: Sums the subsequent expression over the index $i$, which enumerates all charges in the system.

q_i.name: Electric Charge
q_i.description: The electric charge of the $i$-th point charge in the system.

\\Phi.name: Electric Potential
\\Phi.description: The scalar electric potential function. $\Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ is the potential at the location of charge $q_i$ due to all other charges.

\\mathbf{r}_i.name: Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}_i.description: The position vector of the $i$-th point charge.

construction-energy-67a19021.interpretation: The total electrostatic potential energy of a system of discrete charges, denoted by $U$ and measured in Joules ($J$), is calculated using this formula. The expression involves a summation, indexed by $i$, over all charges in the system. For each charge $q_i$ located at a position $\mathbf{r}_i$, it is multiplied by the scalar electric potential $\Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ at that location. This potential $\Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ is generated by all *other* charges in the system (i.e., all $q_j$ where $j \neq i$). The product $q_i \Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ represents the work done to bring charge $q_i$ from infinity to its final position $\mathbf{r}_i$ in the presence of the other assembled charges. The factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ is essential to correct for double-counting the interaction energy of each pair of charges. A naive summation $\sum_i q_i \Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ would count the interaction between $q_i$ and $q_j$ once in the term for $i$ and again in the term for $j$.
construction-energy-67a19021.symmetry_origin: Conservation of energy, which arises from the time-translation invariance of the physical laws governing the electrostatic system, as described by Noether's theorem.
construction-energy-67a19021.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where all charges are infinitely separated ($|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j| \to \infty$ for all $i \neq j$), the potential $\Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ at each charge's location due to the others approaches zero, and thus the total energy $U \to 0$. This formula is valid for static or quasi-static systems where charge velocities are negligible ($v \ll c$). It is a classical result and does not account for quantum effects ($\hbar \to 0$).
construction-energy-67a19021.conceptual_definition: The total electrostatic potential energy, $U$, of a system of discrete point charges is defined as one-half of the sum of the products of each charge $q_i$ and the electric potential $\Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ at its position. The potential $\Phi(\mathbf{r}_i)$ is generated by all other charges in the system.
construction-energy-67a19021.intuitive_summary: This formula represents the total 'assembly cost' in energy to build a configuration of charges. The factor of one-half is crucial because it prevents double-counting the interaction energy between any given pair of charges, similar to how one calculates the number of handshakes in a group.
construction-energy-67a19021.description: Calculates the total potential energy stored in a system of discrete point charges, representing the total work required to assemble the configuration by bringing each charge from infinity.

faraday-origin-92580606.title: Gauss's Law for Magnetism (Differential Form)

\\nabla \\cdot.name: Divergence Operator
\\nabla \\cdot.description: Measures the magnitude of a vector field's source or sink at a given point.

\\mathbf{B}.name: Magnetic Field Vector
\\mathbf{B}.description: A vector field that describes the magnetic influence on moving electric charges, electric currents, and magnetic materials.

0.name: Zero Scalar
0.description: Represents the absence of a net magnetic source or sink at any point in space.

faraday-origin-92580606.interpretation:
The equation $
abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$ describes a fundamental property of the magnetic field. The symbol $
abla \cdot$ represents the divergence operator, which measures the net outflow of a vector field from an infinitesimal point. The vector $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, measured in Tesla ($T$). The equation states that the divergence of the magnetic field is zero everywhere. This has the profound implication that there are no 'sources' or 'sinks' for the magnetic field. Unlike electric fields, which can originate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges (as described by Gauss's Law for electricity, $
abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = ho/\varepsilon_0$), magnetic fields do not arise from magnetic charges, also known as magnetic monopoles. Consequently, magnetic field lines must always form closed loops.
faraday-origin-92580606.symmetry_origin:
Gauge symmetry of electromagnetism. This law is a necessary condition for the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ to be derivable from a magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ (i.e., $\mathbf{B} = 
abla 	imes \mathbf{A}$), which is a cornerstone of gauge theory. The law follows directly from the mathematical identity that the divergence of a curl is always zero ($
abla \cdot (
abla 	imes \mathbf{A}) \equiv 0$).
faraday-origin-92580606.limits_and_boundary: This law is considered exact within the domain of classical and relativistic electrodynamics. It holds at all scales and velocities. Its only hypothetical boundary condition would be the discovery of magnetic monopoles, which would modify the equation to $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \rho_m$, where $\rho_m$ is the magnetic charge density. To date, no such monopoles have been experimentally confirmed.
faraday-origin-92580606.conceptual_definition: This law postulates that the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ has zero divergence at every point in space. This is the mathematical expression of the empirical observation that there are no magnetic monopoles (isolated north or south poles), and as a result, magnetic field lines must always form closed loops.
faraday-origin-92580606.intuitive_summary: Imagine magnetic field lines as continuous, unbreakable loops. This equation is the mathematical rule stating that you can never find a starting or ending point for these loops, unlike electric field lines which can start on positive charges and end on negative ones.
faraday-origin-92580606.description: One of the four Maxwell's equations, this law states that the magnetic field is a solenoidal (divergence-free) vector field, implying the non-existence of magnetic monopoles.

lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.title: Polytropic Equation of State

P.name: Pressure
P.description: The thermodynamic pressure of the polytropic fluid.

K.name: Polytropic constant
K.description: A proportionality constant related to the entropy and composition of the fluid. Its units depend on the value of n.

\\rho.name: Density
\\rho.description: The mass density of the polytropic fluid.

n.name: Polytropic index
n.description: A dimensionless number that characterizes the polytropic process and the stiffness of the equation of state.

lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.interpretation: In the equation $P = K \rho^{1+1/n}$, the pressure $P$ represents the thermodynamic pressure within a self-gravitating fluid, such as a star, which counteracts the inward pull of gravity. The density $\rho$ is the mass per unit volume of the fluid at a given point. The constant $K$ is the polytropic constant, a proportionality factor that depends on the specific entropy and composition of the fluid. The exponent $1 + 1/n$ defines the 'stiffness' of the equation of state. The dimensionless parameter $n$ is the polytropic index, which parameterizes the relationship. Different values of $n$ correspond to different physical models for the stellar interior: $n=0$ models an incompressible fluid with constant density; $n=1.5$ (corresponding to an adiabatic index $\gamma = 5/3$) models a non-relativistic degenerate gas, as found in white dwarfs; and $n=3$ (corresponding to $\gamma = 4/3$) models a highly relativistic degenerate gas or a star dominated by radiation pressure, relevant for massive white dwarfs and the cores of neutron stars.
lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.symmetry_origin: This equation is not derived from a fundamental symmetry. It is a phenomenological or effective model (a constitutive relation) that simplifies complex microphysics into a macroscopic relationship between pressure and density. It is an assumed property of the fluid under consideration.
lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.limits_and_boundary: For $n \to \infty$, the exponent $1+1/n \to 1$, yielding $P = K\rho$. This corresponds to an isothermal gas. For $n=0$, the model represents an incompressible fluid where density $\rho$ is constant, and the pressure is determined by hydrostatic equilibrium, not this equation. The model is physically relevant for polytropic indices in the range $0 \le n < 5$. For $n \ge 5$, the solution to the Lane-Emden equation yields a star with infinite radius, which is unphysical.
lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.conceptual_definition: The polytropic equation of state, expressed as $P = K\rho^{1+1/n}$, provides a simplified model for the relationship between pressure $P$ and density $\rho$ within a fluid, particularly in astrophysical contexts like stars. It assumes that the pressure is proportional to the density raised to a constant power, where the exponent is determined by the polytropic index $n$. This relation is a foundational assumption for deriving the Lane-Emden equation, which describes the structure of a polytropic sphere in hydrostatic equilibrium.
lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.intuitive_summary: Imagine squeezing a ball of gas. This formula describes a simple rule for how much the pressure inside increases as you compress it (increase its density). The specific 'stiffness' of the gas—how much pressure builds up for a given compression—is captured by a single number, the polytropic index $n$.
lane-emden-basis-fc18ebf9.description: A thermodynamic equation of state that models a self-gravitating fluid by relating its pressure to its density through a power law, characterized by a constant polytropic index.

contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.title: Phase Velocity

v_p.name: Phase Velocity
v_p.description: The velocity at which a point of constant phase of a wave propagates.

\\omega.name: Angular Frequency
\\omega.description: The rate of change of the wave's phase with respect to time, equal to $2\pi$ times the frequency $f$.

k.name: Angular Wavenumber
k.description: The spatial frequency of the wave, equal to $2\pi$ divided by the wavelength $\lambda$.

contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.interpretation: The equation for phase speed is given by $v_p = \frac{\omega}{k}$. Here, $\omega$ represents the angular frequency of the wave, measured in radians per second (rad/s), which quantifies the rate of phase change in time. The variable $k$ is the angular wavenumber, measured in radians per meter (rad/m), which quantifies the rate of phase change in space. The wavenumber is related to the wavelength $\lambda$ by the equation $k = 2\pi/\lambda$. The phase speed $v_p$ is fundamentally the ratio of the wave's temporal oscillation rate to its spatial oscillation rate. Its units are meters per second (m/s).
contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.symmetry_origin: The existence of well-defined frequency $\omega$ and wavenumber $k$ for a plane wave is a direct consequence of translational symmetry in time and space, respectively. Via Noether's theorem, these symmetries correspond to the conservation of energy and momentum, to which $\omega$ and $k$ are proportional in quantum mechanics ($E=\hbar\omega$, $\mathbf{p}=\hbar\mathbf{k}$).
contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.limits_and_boundary: In a non-dispersive medium, the ratio $\omega/k$ is constant, so the phase velocity $v_p$ is independent of frequency. In a dispersive medium, $\omega(k)$ is a non-linear function, making $v_p$ frequency-dependent. For electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, $v_p = c$. For a relativistic massive particle with velocity $v$, its de Broglie wave has a phase velocity $v_p = E/p = (\gamma m c^2) / (\gamma m v) = c^2/v$, which is always greater than $c$. This does not violate causality, as information propagates at the group velocity $v_g$, not the phase velocity.
contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.conceptual_definition: The phase velocity $v_p$ is defined as the speed at which a point of constant phase, $\phi(x, t) = kx - \omega t = \text{const}$, propagates. By taking the total time derivative and setting it to zero, $\frac{d\phi}{dt} = 0$, we find $\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = 0$. Substituting the partial derivatives yields $k \frac{dx}{dt} - \omega = 0$. Since $\frac{dx}{dt}$ is the velocity of this constant-phase point, we identify it as $v_p$, leading directly to the relation $v_p = \omega/k$.
contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.intuitive_summary: Imagine a series of waves on water. The phase velocity is the speed of a single crest or trough. It's the speed you would need to travel to stay 'locked' onto a specific point of the wave's shape as it moves.
contour-of-constant-phase-ca83865e.description: Defines the propagation speed of a point of constant phase for a monochromatic wave, relating its temporal frequency to its spatial frequency.

vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.title: Baryon Number Violation Rate via Sphaleron Tunneling

\\Gamma_{B}.name: Baryon Number Violation Rate
\\Gamma_{B}.description: The rate of change of baryon number due to sphaleron transitions.

\\alpha_W.name: Weak Fine-Structure Constant
\\alpha_W.description: The coupling constant for the SU(2) gauge interaction, analogous to the fine-structure constant of electromagnetism. Defined as $\alpha_W = g_W^2 / (4\pi)$.

\\exp.name: Exponential Function
\\exp.description: The base of the natural logarithm raised to a power.

\\propto.name: Proportionality Operator
\\propto.description: Indicates that the two sides of the relation are proportional, differing only by a constant prefactor.

vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.interpretation: The formula $\Gamma_{B} \propto \exp(-4\pi/\alpha_W)$ gives the rate of baryon number violation, $\Gamma_B$, at zero temperature. The process is a form of quantum tunneling between distinct electroweak vacuum states. The rate is exponentially suppressed by the factor in the exponent, where $\alpha_W$ is the weak fine-structure constant, defined as $\alpha_W = g_W^2 / (4\pi)$ with $g_W$ being the SU(2) gauge coupling. The term in the exponent, $4\pi/\alpha_W$, is twice the Euclidean action of the instanton ($2S_{instanton}$), the field configuration describing the tunneling event. Since $\alpha_W \approx 1/29.5$, the exponent is extremely large and negative, rendering the rate $\Gamma_B$ practically zero. This ensures the stability of baryons like the proton over cosmological timescales against this specific decay channel.
vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.symmetry_origin: This process is a physical manifestation of the Adler-Bell-Jackiw (ABJ) chiral anomaly in the electroweak sector. While baryon number is an accidental symmetry of the classical Standard Model Lagrangian, it is violated at the quantum level by this anomaly for the SU(2)_L gauge group. The sphaleron transition changes the Chern-Simons number of the gauge fields, which in turn leads to a corresponding change in the number of fermions.
vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.limits_and_boundary: In the zero-temperature limit ($T \to 0$), the rate $\Gamma_B$ is given by this formula and is infinitesimally small, effectively conserving baryon number. In the high-temperature limit ($T \gg M_W / \alpha_W$), relevant to the early universe, thermal fluctuations dominate over quantum tunneling. The transition rate is no longer exponentially suppressed and becomes significant, scaling approximately as $\Gamma_{sph} \propto (\alpha_W T)^4$. In the classical limit ($\hbar \to 0$), quantum tunneling is forbidden, and thus $\Gamma_B \to 0$.
vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.conceptual_definition: In electroweak theory, the vacuum possesses a periodic structure with degenerate states separated by a finite energy barrier. A sphaleron is a static, unstable field configuration at the peak of this barrier. The rate $\Gamma_B$ quantifies the probability of quantum tunneling between these vacua, a process which violates baryon number ($B$) and lepton number ($L$) conservation according to the rule $\Delta B = \Delta L$. This rate is exponentially suppressed by a factor related to the Euclidean action of the instanton, which describes the tunneling path.
vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.intuitive_summary: Imagine the universe's vacuum state as a valley in a vast landscape of identical valleys. To change the fundamental number of baryons (like protons and neutrons), you must 'tunnel' through the mountain to an adjacent valley. This formula shows that the probability of such a tunnel event at zero temperature is astronomically low, making baryon number effectively a conserved quantity in our cold universe. The process is named after the 'sphaleron', which represents the easiest path over the top of the mountain separating the valleys.
vacuum-tunneling-f7885b09.description: This formula provides the zero-temperature rate for baryon number non-conservation in the Standard Model, a non-perturbative quantum tunneling process mediated by sphaleron configurations.

logical-basis-e6586e00.title: Canonical Symplectic 2-Form in Local Coordinates

\\omega.name: Canonical Symplectic 2-Form
\\omega.description: A differential 2-form that endows the phase space with a symplectic structure, defining oriented area elements.

p_i.name: Canonical Momentum
p_i.description: The momentum conjugate to the generalized coordinate $q^i$.

q^i.name: Generalized Coordinate
q^i.description: A coordinate representing a degree of freedom of the system.

dp_i.name: Differential of Canonical Momentum
dp_i.description: A 1-form representing an infinitesimal change in the canonical momentum $p_i$.

dq^i.name: Differential of Generalized Coordinate
dq^i.description: A 1-form representing an infinitesimal change in the generalized coordinate $q^i$.

\\wedge.name: Exterior Product
\\wedge.description: An anti-symmetric product that combines two differential forms to create a higher-degree form.

\\sum.name: Summation
\\sum.description: Summation over all degrees of freedom of the system, typically from $i=1$ to $n$.

logical-basis-e6586e00.interpretation: In this formula, $\omega$ is the canonical symplectic 2-form, a differential 2-form on the phase space manifold. The phase space of a classical mechanical system is constructed from its generalized coordinates $q^i$ and their corresponding conjugate momenta $p_i$. The index $i$ ranges over the $n$ degrees of freedom of the system. The term $dp_i$ represents the differential 1-form for the conjugate momentum of the $i$-th degree of freedom, and $dq^i$ represents the differential 1-form for the $i$-th generalized coordinate. The symbol $\wedge$ denotes the exterior product, an anti-symmetric bilinear operation, which implies $dp_i \wedge dq^i = -dq^i \wedge dp_i$. The summation $\sum$ indicates that $\omega$ is the sum of these elementary symplectic areas over all degrees of freedom. For the phase space to be a symplectic manifold, this 2-form must be closed ($d\omega = 0$) and non-degenerate. This structure is fundamental to Hamiltonian dynamics, as the time evolution of a system is described by a flow generated by a Hamiltonian vector field with respect to this symplectic form.
logical-basis-e6586e00.symmetry_origin: The symplectic form $\omega$ is invariant under canonical transformations (symplectomorphisms), which are the fundamental symmetries of Hamiltonian mechanics. The time evolution of a system, known as Hamiltonian flow, is itself a canonical transformation. This invariance, expressed as $\mathcal{L}_{X_H} \omega = 0$, directly leads to the conservation of phase space volume (Liouville's Theorem).
logical-basis-e6586e00.limits_and_boundary: This is a foundational formula of classical Hamiltonian mechanics. In the classical limit where Planck's constant is negligible ($\hbar \to 0$), this geometric structure provides a complete description of dynamics. The structure is a precursor to quantum mechanics, where the non-zero value of the commutator $[\hat{q}^i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar\delta^i_j$ can be viewed as a quantization of the classical symplectic form.
logical-basis-e6586e00.conceptual_definition: This equation provides the local coordinate representation of the canonical symplectic 2-form $\omega$ on a phase space manifold $M$. For any set of canonical coordinates $(q^1, \dots, q^n, p_1, \dots, p_n)$, $\omega$ is defined as the sum of the exterior products of the differential 1-forms $dp_i$ and $dq^i$. This form is exact, as it can be written as the exterior derivative of the Liouville 1-form $\theta = \sum_i p_i dq^i$, specifically $\omega = d(\sum_i p_i dq^i) = \sum_i dp_i \wedge dq^i$.
logical-basis-e6586e00.intuitive_summary: This formula acts as a geometric 'ruler' for measuring oriented areas in phase space. Each term $dp_i \wedge dq^i$ represents an infinitesimal parallelogram spanned by a change in momentum and a change in position for a single degree of freedom. Summing these areas defines the fundamental structure that governs the flow of physical states, ensuring that phase space volume is conserved over time (Liouville's Theorem).
logical-basis-e6586e00.description: Defines the canonical symplectic 2-form $\omega$ on a classical phase space, providing the geometric foundation for Hamiltonian mechanics in local coordinates $(q^i, p_i)$.

algebraic-duality-4db70c80.title: Metric Tensor Inverse Definition

algebraic-duality-4db70c80.description: This equation defines the contravariant metric tensor as the matrix inverse of the covariant metric tensor, a fundamental algebraic identity in tensor calculus and general relativity.

repulsive-gravity-3202861e.title: Vacuum Energy Density (Cosmological Constant)

\\rho_\\Lambda.name: Vacuum Energy Density
\\rho_\\Lambda.description: The energy density of empty space, also known as dark energy, which is constant throughout spacetime.

\\Lambda.name: Cosmological Constant
\\Lambda.description: A fundamental constant of nature representing the energy density of the vacuum, responsible for the accelerated expansion of the universe.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: The universal speed limit for all energy, matter, and information.

G.name: Newtonian Constant of Gravitation
G.description: The empirical physical constant quantifying the magnitude of the gravitational force between two bodies.

\\pi.name: Pi
\\pi.description: The mathematical constant representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.

repulsive-gravity-3202861e.interpretation:
This equation defines the vacuum energy density $ho_\Lambda$ in terms of the cosmological constant $\Lambda$. The term $ho_\Lambda$ represents the energy density of empty space, with SI units of Joules per cubic meter ($J \cdot m^{-3}$) or kilograms per cubic meter ($kg \cdot m^{-3}$). The cosmological constant $\Lambda$ has units of inverse length squared ($m^{-2}$). The equation arises from incorporating $\Lambda$ into the Einstein Field Equations, $G_{\mu
u} + \Lambda g_{\mu
u} =  rac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu
u}$. By moving the $\Lambda$ term to the right-hand side, it can be interpreted as a contribution to the stress-energy tensor, $T_{\mu
u}^{(\Lambda)} = - rac{\Lambda c^4}{8\pi G} g_{\mu
u}$. The time-time component of this tensor, $T_{00}^{(\Lambda)}$, corresponds to an energy density term $ho_\Lambda c^2$, from which we identify $ho_\Lambda =  rac{\Lambda c^2}{8\pi G}$. A positive $\Lambda$ corresponds to a positive energy density but a negative pressure $p_\Lambda = -ho_\Lambda c^2$, which drives the accelerated expansion of the universe.
repulsive-gravity-3202861e.symmetry_origin: The cosmological constant term $\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ is the most general term that can be added to the Einstein-Hilbert action that preserves the diffeomorphism invariance (general covariance) of the theory and results in second-order field equations. Its inclusion respects the fundamental geometric symmetries of General Relativity.
repulsive-gravity-3202861e.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the cosmological constant approaches zero, $\Lambda \to 0$, the vacuum energy density also vanishes, $\rho_\Lambda \to 0$. This recovers the original formulation of Einstein's field equations for a matter-dominated, decelerating universe. As $\rho_\Lambda$ is considered a constant property of the vacuum, it does not vary with temperature $T$, velocity $v$, or spatial position $r$. The formula is classical; its quantum field theory analogue, calculated from vacuum fluctuations, leads to the cosmological constant problem, predicting a value for $\rho_\Lambda$ that is many orders of magnitude larger than observed.
repulsive-gravity-3202861e.conceptual_definition: The formula $\rho_\Lambda = \frac{\Lambda c^2}{8\pi G}$ establishes a direct proportionality between the vacuum energy density $\rho_\Lambda$ and the cosmological constant $\Lambda$. It quantifies the intrinsic, uniform energy content of empty spacetime, which acts as a source of gravitational repulsion driving the accelerated expansion of the universe.
repulsive-gravity-3202861e.intuitive_summary: Imagine that empty space is not truly empty but possesses a fundamental, built-in energy. This formula calculates the density of that energy. A positive value means that as the universe expands and more 'empty space' is created, more of this energy appears, pushing everything apart at an ever-increasing rate, acting like a form of 'repulsive gravity'.
repulsive-gravity-3202861e.description: This equation defines the energy density of the vacuum, often called dark energy, as a function of the cosmological constant, providing a physical interpretation for this term within general relativity.

robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.title: Robertson Uncertainty Law

\\sigma_A.name: Standard Deviation of A
\\sigma_A.description: The standard deviation of measurements of the observable A, quantifying its uncertainty.

\\sigma_B.name: Standard Deviation of B
\\sigma_B.description: The standard deviation of measurements of the observable B, quantifying its uncertainty.

\\hat{A}.name: Operator A
\\hat{A}.description: The Hermitian operator corresponding to the physical observable A.

\\hat{B}.name: Operator B
\\hat{B}.description: The Hermitian operator corresponding to the physical observable B.

[\\hat{A}, \\hat{B}].name: Commutator of A and B
[\\hat{A}, \\hat{B}].unit: Product of units of A and B
[\\hat{A}, \\hat{B}].description: The commutator operator, defined as $\hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}$, which measures the degree of non-commutativity between the two operators.

\\langle \\cdot \\rangle.name: Expectation Value
\\langle \\cdot \\rangle.description: The expectation value of an operator in a given quantum state, representing the average result of a large number of measurements.

robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.interpretation: In the Robertson Uncertainty Law, $\sigma_A$ represents the standard deviation (uncertainty) of the observable corresponding to the operator $\hat{A}$, and $\sigma_B$ represents the standard deviation of the observable corresponding to the operator $\hat{B}$. The term $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]$ denotes the commutator of the operators, defined as $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}$. The expression $\langle [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \rangle$ is the expectation value of this commutator in the quantum state under consideration. The factor of $1/(2i)$ is present because the commutator of two Hermitian operators is anti-Hermitian, and its expectation value is purely imaginary; this factor makes the result a real number. The law states that the product of the uncertainties $\sigma_A \sigma_B$ is bounded below. If the operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ commute, their commutator is zero, and thus the product of uncertainties can be zero, meaning both observables can be known simultaneously with perfect precision.
robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.symmetry_origin: This law does not arise from a conservation law via Noether's theorem. Instead, it is a direct mathematical consequence of the non-commutative algebraic structure of quantum mechanics, where physical observables are represented by operators on a Hilbert space that do not, in general, commute.
robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit where Planck's constant $\hbar \to 0$, the commutator $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]$ approaches zero (as $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \to i\hbar \{A, B\}_{PB}$), so the lower bound on uncertainty vanishes. This recovers the classical mechanics principle that all observables can be measured simultaneously with arbitrary precision. If the operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ commute, i.e., $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = 0$, the lower bound is zero, indicating that there is no fundamental restriction on the simultaneous measurement of the corresponding observables.
robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.conceptual_definition: The Robertson Uncertainty Law provides a precise mathematical formulation for the inherent trade-off in the simultaneous measurement of two non-commuting quantum observables. It states that for any two Hermitian operators, $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$, the product of their standard deviations, $\sigma_A$ and $\sigma_B$, in a given quantum state must be greater than or equal to the magnitude of half the expectation value of their commutator, $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]$.
robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.intuitive_summary: Imagine two properties of a quantum particle, like its position and momentum. This law says you can't know both perfectly at the same time. There's a fundamental trade-off: the more precisely you measure one, the fuzzier your knowledge of the other becomes. The law quantifies this 'fuzziness trade-off' for any pair of incompatible properties, linking it to how much their measurement procedures interfere with each other (their non-commutativity).
robertson-uncertainty-law-699c7364.description: A fundamental principle in quantum mechanics that generalizes the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, establishing a lower bound for the product of the uncertainties of any two observables based on the expectation value of their commutator.

friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.title: Second Friedmann Equation (Acceleration Equation)
friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.interpretation: The left side of the equation, $\ddot{a}/a$, represents the acceleration of the universe's expansion, normalized by the scale factor $a$. A positive value indicates accelerating expansion, while a negative value indicates decelerating expansion. The first term on the right side, $-\frac{4\pi G}{3} (\rho + \frac{3P}{c^2})$, describes the deceleration caused by the universe's contents. Here, $G$ is the gravitational constant, $\rho$ is the total energy density, and $P$ is the total pressure. The term $(\rho + 3P/c^2)$ acts as the 'active gravitational mass', where strong positive pressure contributes to gravitational attraction. The final term, $\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$, represents the contribution from the cosmological constant $\Lambda$, which acts as a repulsive force (equivalent to a fluid with negative pressure $P_\Lambda = -\rho_\Lambda c^2$), driving accelerated expansion. The sign of the overall acceleration is determined by the balance between the decelerating effects of matter/energy and the accelerating effect of the cosmological constant.
friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.symmetry_origin: This equation is a consequence of applying the principle of general covariance (the laws of physics are the same for all observers) to a spacetime that exhibits maximal spatial symmetry, i.e., homogeneity and isotropy, as described by the FLRW metric.
friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.limits_and_boundary: In a matter-dominated universe where pressure is negligible ($P \approx 0$) and $\Lambda=0$, the equation simplifies to $\ddot{a}/a = -4\pi G \rho / 3$, predicting deceleration. In a universe dominated by the cosmological constant (where $\rho \to \rho_\Lambda$ and $P \to P_\Lambda = -\rho_\Lambda c^2$), the equation yields $\ddot{a}/a \approx \Lambda c^2 / 3 > 0$, leading to exponential, accelerated expansion (a de Sitter universe). For a radiation-dominated universe, where $P = \rho c^2/3$, the source term $(\rho c^2 + 3P)$ becomes $2\rho c^2 > 0$, also causing deceleration.

a.name: Cosmic Scale Factor
a.description: A function of time, $a(t)$, which represents the relative expansion of the universe. $\dot{a}$ is its first time derivative (expansion rate) and $\ddot{a}$ is its second time derivative (expansion acceleration).

\\pi.name: Pi
\\pi.description: The mathematical constant representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.

c.name: Speed of Light
c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum.

\\rho.name: Total Energy Density
\\rho.description: The total energy density of the universe, including matter, radiation, and dark energy.

P.name: Total Pressure
P.description: The total pressure of the cosmic fluid, contributed by all components of the universe.

\\Lambda.name: Cosmological Constant
\\Lambda.description: A constant term representing the energy density of the vacuum (dark energy), which drives the accelerated expansion of the universe.

friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.conceptual_definition: Derived from the Einstein Field Equations for a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric, the Second Friedmann Equation is a dynamical equation governing the acceleration of the cosmic scale factor, $a(t)$. It relates the second time derivative of the scale factor to the active gravitational mass density, $(\rho + 3P/c^2)$, and the cosmological constant, $\Lambda$.
friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.intuitive_summary: This equation represents a cosmic 'tug-of-war'. The expansion of the universe is slowed down by the gravitational pull of all matter and energy ($\rho$) and its associated pressure ($P$). However, a mysterious 'dark energy', represented by the cosmological constant ($\Lambda$), provides a constant repulsive force, pushing the universe to expand at an accelerating rate.
friedmann-acceleration-equation-expansio.description: A fundamental equation in physical cosmology that describes the acceleration of the expansion of space in a homogeneous and isotropic universe, governed by its energy density, pressure, and the cosmological constant.

boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.title: Integrated Boltzmann Equation for Cosmic Relic Abundance
boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.interpretation: The left side of the equation, $\frac{dn_\chi}{dt} + 3Hn_\chi$, represents the total rate of change of the number density of $\chi$ particles, $n_\chi$, in a comoving volume. The term $\frac{dn_\chi}{dt}$ is the explicit time derivative of the number density, while the $3Hn_\chi$ term accounts for the dilution of particles due to the Hubble expansion, where $H$ is the Hubble parameter. The right side, $-\langle \sigma v \rangle [ n_\chi^2 - (n_\chi^{eq})^2 ]$, quantifies the net effect of particle interactions. The quantity $\langle \sigma v \rangle$ is the thermally averaged annihilation cross-section times velocity, setting the fundamental interaction strength. The $n_\chi^2$ term is proportional to the annihilation rate (a loss term), while the $(n_\chi^{eq})^2$ term is proportional to the creation rate from the thermal bath (a source term), where $n_\chi^{eq}$ is the number density the species would have in full thermal equilibrium. The equation thus describes how the actual number density $n_\chi$ deviates from and relaxes towards its equilibrium value $n_\chi^{eq}$.
boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.symmetry_origin: The equation's structure arises from the combination of the Cosmological Principle (homogeneity and isotropy, leading to the FLRW metric and the $3H$ expansion term) and the principles of statistical mechanics in a non-equilibrium context (the collision term on the right-hand side).
boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.limits_and_boundary: In the early, hot universe where temperature $T$ is high, interaction rates are much faster than the expansion rate ($\Gamma \gg H$). The system remains in thermal equilibrium, so $n_\chi \approx n_\chi^{eq}$ and the right-hand side is approximately zero. In the late, cold universe (after 'freeze-out'), the temperature is too low for significant creation or annihilation, so the interaction rate is negligible ($\Gamma \ll H$). The right-hand side vanishes, and the equation becomes $\frac{dn_\chi}{dt} + 3Hn_\chi \approx 0$, indicating that the number of particles in a comoving volume becomes constant, and the physical number density $n_\chi$ simply dilutes as the universe expands.

n_\\chi.name: Number Density of Particle Species Chi
n_\\chi.description: The number of particles of species χ per unit physical volume.

t.name: Cosmic Time
t.description: Time coordinate in the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric.

H.name: Hubble Parameter
H.description: The rate of expansion of the universe, defined as $H = \dot{a}/a$, where $a$ is the scale factor.

\\langle \\sigma v \\rangle.name: Thermally Averaged Annihilation Cross-Section
\\langle \\sigma v \\rangle.description: The annihilation cross-section (σ) times relative velocity (v), averaged over the thermal distribution of the particle species.

n_\\chi^{eq}.name: Equilibrium Number Density
n_\\chi^{eq}.description: The number density the particle species χ would have if it were in perfect thermal equilibrium with the cosmic plasma at a given temperature.

\\frac{d}{dt}.name: Time Derivative
\\frac{d}{dt}.description: The operator for the rate of change with respect to cosmic time.

boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.conceptual_definition: The Integrated Boltzmann Equation is a rate equation that models the time evolution of the number density, $n_\chi$, of a particle species $\chi$ within a homogeneous and isotropic expanding universe. It equates the rate of change of particle number in a comoving volume to the net rate of particle annihilation and creation. The equation is fundamental for calculating the relic abundance of thermally produced particles, such as dark matter.
boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.intuitive_summary: Imagine a box full of particles that is expanding along with the universe. The particles naturally spread out as the box grows, reducing their density (this is the 'Hubble drag' term). Simultaneously, particles can collide and annihilate each other, while the background thermal energy can create new pairs. This equation is the master accountant that tracks the balance between dilution, annihilation, and creation to determine how many particles survive to the present day.
boltzmann-equation-integrated-cosmology-.description: A differential equation describing the evolution of the number density of a particle species in the early universe, accounting for dilution from cosmic expansion and changes from particle annihilation and creation processes.

nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.title: The Central Equation of the Nearly-Free Electron Model
nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.interpretation: The equation $(\lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} - E) C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} + \sum_{\mathbf{G'}} V_{\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G'}} C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G'}} = 0$ represents a system of coupled linear secular equations for the expansion coefficients $C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$ of a Bloch electron wavefunction. The kinetic energy term $(\lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} - E) C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$ represents the unperturbed free-electron energy $\lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} = \frac{\hbar^2 |\mathbf{k} - \mathbf{G}|^2}{2m}$ relative to the total energy $E$. The summation term $\sum_{\mathbf{G'}} V_{\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G'}} C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G'}}$ calculates the effect of Bragg scattering, which couples plane-wave components $C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G'}}$ via the Fourier components $V_{\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G'}}$ of the periodic lattice potential $V(\mathbf{r})$. Non-trivial solutions for the coefficients $C$ exist only when the secular determinant of the system vanishes, a condition that yields the allowed energy eigenvalues $E(\mathbf{k})$ and reveals the formation of energy band gaps at the Brillouin zone boundaries.
nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.symmetry_origin: The equation is a direct consequence of the discrete translational symmetry of the crystal lattice. This symmetry, formalized by Bloch's Theorem, dictates that the electronic wavefunction must be a plane wave modulated by a periodic function. The use of a Fourier series over reciprocal lattice vectors ($\mathbf{G}$) to represent the potential and wavefunction is the mathematical embodiment of this periodicity.
nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the periodic potential vanishes ($V_{\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G'}} \to 0$), the coupling term disappears. The equation reduces to $(\lambda_{\mathbf{k}} - E)C_{\mathbf{k}} = 0$, which yields the parabolic energy-momentum relation $E(\mathbf{k}) = \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}$ of a free electron. At the boundaries of the Brillouin zone (e.g., where $k \approx \pi/a$), the free-electron energies $\lambda_{\mathbf{k}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$ become degenerate, leading to strong mixing by the potential $V$ and the opening of an energy band gap.

\\lambda_{\\mathbf{k}-\\mathbf{G}}.name: Free-electron kinetic energy
\\lambda_{\\mathbf{k}-\\mathbf{G}}.description: The kinetic energy of a free-electron plane wave with wavevector $\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}$.

E.name: Energy eigenvalue
E.description: The total energy of the electron in the crystal, which is to be solved for.

C_{\\mathbf{k}-\\mathbf{G}}.name: Fourier coefficient
C_{\\mathbf{k}-\\mathbf{G}}.description: The expansion coefficient for the plane wave component with wavevector $\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}$ in the Bloch wavefunction.

V_{\\mathbf{G}-\\mathbf{G'}}.name: Potential Fourier component
V_{\\mathbf{G}-\\mathbf{G'}}.description: The Fourier coefficient of the periodic lattice potential, which couples plane wave states differing by the reciprocal lattice vector $\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G'}$.

\\mathbf{k}.name: Crystal momentum wavevector
\\mathbf{k}.description: The wavevector of the electron, typically restricted to the first Brillouin zone.

\\mathbf{G}.name: Reciprocal lattice vector
\\mathbf{G}.description: A vector in the reciprocal lattice, defining the periodicity of the Fourier expansion.

\\sum_{\\mathbf{G'}}.name: Summation operator

nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.conceptual_definition: This equation is the time-independent Schrödinger equation for an electron in a periodic potential, transformed into reciprocal (momentum) space. It presents the Hamiltonian as an infinite matrix acting on a vector of Fourier coefficients, $C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$, which represent the amplitudes of plane waves comprising the electron's Bloch state. The eigenvalues of this matrix equation are the allowed electron energies $E(\mathbf{k})$.
nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.intuitive_summary: Imagine an electron moving freely through space as a simple wave. When this electron enters a crystal, its wave is scattered by the periodic array of atoms. This equation describes how all the scattered versions of the electron wave mix together. When the electron's wavelength perfectly matches the spacing of the atoms (a condition for Bragg diffraction), the mixing is very strong, and it opens up a 'band gap'—a range of energies the electron is forbidden to have.
nearly-free-electron-central-equation-89.description: The secular equation governing the Fourier components of an electronic wavefunction in a weak periodic crystal potential, which determines the electronic band structure and energy gaps in solids.

jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.title: The Jarlskog Invariant: A Rephasing-Invariant Measure of CP Violation
jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.equation: J = \operatorname{Im}\left( V_{ud} V_{cs} V_{us}^* V_{cd}^* \right) = c_{12} c_{23} c_{13}^2 s_{12} s_{23} s_{13} \sin\delta_{13}
jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.interpretation: The quantity $J$ is a rephasing-invariant measure of CP violation, meaning its value is independent of the phase conventions chosen for the quark fields. The elements $V_{ij}$ belong to the 3x3 unitary Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix, which describes the mixing between the weak and mass eigenstates of quarks. A non-zero value of $J$ requires at least three generations of quarks and a non-trivial complex phase in the CKM matrix, which is the sole source of CP violation in the Standard Model's quark sector. The expression $c_{12} c_{23} c_{13}^2 s_{12} s_{23} s_{13} \sin\delta_{13}$ represents $J$ in the standard Particle Data Group (PDG) parameterization of the CKM matrix, where $c_{ij} = \cos\theta_{ij}$ and $s_{ij} = \sin\theta_{ij}$ are the cosines and sines of the mixing angles $\theta_{ij}$, and $\delta_{13}$ is the CP-violating phase.
jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.symmetry_origin: The existence of a non-zero Jarlskog invariant $J$ arises from the complex phase in the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix, which is a physical parameter that cannot be removed by rephasing the quark fields. This phase breaks the Charge-Parity (CP) symmetry, a discrete symmetry combining charge conjugation (C) and parity inversion (P).
jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.limits_and_boundary: If any of the mixing angles $\theta_{ij}$ were zero or $\pi/2$, or if the CP-violating phase $\delta_{13}$ were zero or $\pi$, the Jarlskog invariant $J$ would be zero, and there would be no CP violation in the quark sector of the Standard Model. The existence of CP violation requires all three generations of quarks to mix with each other ($s_{12}, s_{23}, s_{13} \neq 0$) and a non-trivial phase ($\sin\delta_{13} \neq 0$). In a hypothetical two-generation model, the CKM matrix can always be made real, resulting in $J=0$.

jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.conceptual_definition: The Jarlskog Invariant, denoted by $J$, is a specific combination of elements from the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix $V$ that quantifies the strength of CP violation. It is defined as the imaginary part of a particular quartet of CKM elements: $J = \operatorname{Im}(V_{ij} V_{kl} V_{il}^* V_{kj}^*)$, where $i,j,k,l$ are distinct quark generation indices. For three generations, this simplifies to the canonical form $J = \operatorname{Im}(V_{ud} V_{cs} V_{us}^* V_{cd}^*)$. Its value is independent of any phase redefinitions of the quark fields, making it a physically observable quantity. A non-zero value of $J$ is a necessary condition for CP violation in the Standard Model's quark sector.
jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.intuitive_summary: Imagine the mixing between different types of quarks as a complex rotation in an abstract space. The Jarlskog Invariant, $J$, measures the 'twist' or 'non-planarity' of this rotation. If all the rotations happened in a single flat plane (no complex phase), $J$ would be zero, and matter and antimatter would behave identically. A non-zero $J$ signifies a fundamental, measurable asymmetry, which is a key ingredient for explaining why the universe is dominated by matter.
jarlskog-invariant-cp-phase-be333aaf.description: A fundamental quantity in particle physics that provides a phase-convention-independent measure of the magnitude of Charge-Parity (CP) violation in the quark sector of the Standard Model, derived from the elements of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix.

mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.title: MOND Interpolating Function for Mass Discrepancy
mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.interpretation: The formula states that the ratio of the total dynamical mass $M_{\text{dyn}}$ to the baryonic mass $M_{\text{bar}}$ is equal to the ratio of the observed gravitational acceleration $g$ to the Newtonian acceleration predicted from baryonic matter alone, $g_{\text{bar}}$. This ratio is given by the inverse of a specific 'simple' interpolating function, $\left[1 - \exp\left(-\sqrt{\frac{g_{\text{bar}}}{a_0}}\right)\right]^{-1}$. Here, $a_0$ is the characteristic acceleration scale of MOND, approximately $1.2 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m/s}^2$. This form is one of several possible interpolating functions in MOND that connect the Newtonian and modified gravity regimes.
mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.symmetry_origin: Phenomenological modification of dynamics; not derived from a fundamental symmetry principle. It is constructed to preserve desired symmetries like space-time invariance while modifying gravitational dynamics.
mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.limits_and_boundary: In the high-acceleration limit where $g_{\text{bar}} \gg a_0$, the exponential term $\exp(-\sqrt{g_{\text{bar}}/a_0}) \to 0$, causing the expression to approach $1$. This recovers Newtonian dynamics, where $M_{\text{dyn}} = M_{\text{bar}}$ and $g = g_{\text{bar}}$. In the low-acceleration (deep-MOND) limit where $g_{\text{bar}} \ll a_0$, a Taylor expansion of the exponential ($e^{-x} \approx 1-x$) yields $g/g_{\text{bar}} \approx (\sqrt{g_{\text{bar}}/a_0})^{-1}$, which simplifies to the core MOND relation $g = \sqrt{g_{\text{bar}} a_0}$.

mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.conceptual_definition: This equation defines the ratio of total dynamical mass ($M_{\text{dyn}}$) to the observed baryonic mass ($M_{\text{bar}}$) within the framework of Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). This ratio, equivalent to the ratio of the true gravitational acceleration ($g$) to the expected Newtonian acceleration from baryons alone ($g_{\text{bar}}$), is expressed through a specific interpolating function involving the fundamental MOND acceleration constant, $a_0$. The function smoothly transitions from the Newtonian regime ($g_{\text{bar}} \gg a_0$) to the modified deep-MOND regime ($g_{\text{bar}} \ll a_0$).
mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.intuitive_summary: In galaxies, the gravity we observe is stronger than what the visible matter (stars, gas) can account for. MOND suggests that instead of adding invisible 'dark matter,' we should modify the law of gravity itself when accelerations are very weak. This formula is a mathematical recipe that specifies exactly how much 'extra' gravity (and thus, 'extra' apparent mass) is generated, based on how weak the gravitational pull from the visible matter is.
mass-discrepancy-identity-1-a3086ae8-22e.description: This formula provides a specific mathematical relationship proposed by Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) to explain the observed mass discrepancy in galaxies, connecting the total dynamical mass to the visible baryonic mass via an interpolating function dependent on gravitational acceleration.

identical-particle-symmetry-identity-1-b.title: Symmetric and Antisymmetric Wave Functions
identical-particle-symmetry-identity-1-b.interpretation: $x_1, x_2$ are the coordinates of particles 1 and 2, $\phi_a, \phi_b$ are single-particle states, and the $1/\sqrt{2}$ factor normalizes the wave function.
identical-particle-symmetry-identity-1-b.symmetry_origin: Particle exchange indistinguishability, which acts as a fundamental symmetry of nature.

constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.title: Generalized Constraint Force via Lagrange Multipliers
constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.interpretation: The term $F_j^c$ is the $j$-th component of the generalized force of constraint. The index $\alpha$ iterates through each of the system's constraint equations, denoted by $f_\alpha = 0$. The scalar $\lambda_\alpha$ is the Lagrange multiplier for the $\alpha$-th constraint, representing the magnitude of the force required to enforce it. The term $\frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial q_j}$ is the component of the gradient of the constraint function $f_\alpha$ in the direction of the generalized coordinate $q_j$. The gradient vector itself is normal to the constraint surface in configuration space. Thus, the equation states that the total generalized constraint force is a sum of forces, each normal to one of the constraint surfaces.
constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.symmetry_origin: This formula is not a direct result of a symmetry via Noether's theorem. Instead, it is a mathematical construct arising from D'Alembert's principle and the method of Lagrange multipliers, used to incorporate geometric constraints into the equations of motion. The underlying principle is that ideal constraint forces are orthogonal to any virtual displacement allowed by the constraints.
constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.limits_and_boundary: This is a formula of classical mechanics and does not have meaningful limits as $\hbar \to 0$ or $v \to c$. If all Lagrange multipliers $\lambda_\alpha$ are zero, it signifies the absence of constraint forces, and the system evolves as if unconstrained. The formula is primarily applicable to holonomic constraints, which are expressible as algebraic equations $f_\alpha(\mathbf{q}, t) = 0$.

F_j^c.name: Generalized Force of Constraint
F_j^c.description: The j-th component of the generalized force that enforces the system's constraints. Unit is Newton if q_j is a length, or N*m if q_j is an angle.

\\lambda_\\alpha.name: Lagrange Multiplier
\\lambda_\\alpha.description: A scalar factor representing the magnitude of the force of constraint associated with the alpha-th constraint equation. Assumes the constraint function f_alpha has units of length.

f_\\alpha.description: The alpha-th holonomic constraint equation of the form f_alpha(q, t) = 0. Conventionally given units of length.

q_j.name: Generalized Coordinate

\\partial.name: Partial Derivative Operator

\\sum_\\alpha.name: Summation Operator
\\sum_\\alpha.description: Operator that sums a series of terms over the index alpha, which enumerates the constraints.

constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.conceptual_definition: In a system described by generalized coordinates $q_j$ and subject to holonomic constraints $f_\alpha(\mathbf{q}, t) = 0$, the generalized force of constraint $F_j^c$ is the force component along the $q_j$ direction that enforces these constraints. It is mathematically expressed as the sum over all constraints $\alpha$ of the product of a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda_\alpha$ and the partial derivative of the constraint function $f_\alpha$ with respect to $q_j$. This construction ensures that the constraint forces are always perpendicular to the surfaces of constant constraint, and thus perform no work under virtual displacements, consistent with D'Alembert's principle.
constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.intuitive_summary: This formula calculates the 'keep-on-the-track' forces in a constrained system, like the force a roller coaster track exerts on the car. Each constraint (a piece of the track's path) contributes a force whose strength is given by a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$ and whose direction is perpendicular to the allowed motion.
constraint-forces-identity-1-a399e7ca-4a.description: Defines the generalized force of constraint in Lagrangian mechanics as a linear combination of the gradients of the constraint equations, weighted by Lagrange multipliers.

angular-momentum-component.title: Angular Momentum Component
angular-momentum-component.conceptual_definition: This formula quantifies the component of angular momentum of a rigid body along a specific axis. It relates this angular momentum component to the components of the body's angular velocity and its inertia tensor. The inertia tensor encapsulates how the mass of the body is distributed relative to the chosen coordinate system.
angular-momentum-component.intuitive_summary: The angular momentum along an axis is a weighted sum of the angular velocity components, where the weights are determined by the body's resistance to rotation around those axes.
angular-momentum-component.interpretation: The formula defines the $i$-th component of the angular momentum vector, denoted as $L_i$, which is a vector quantity representing the rotational inertia of a body. It is calculated by summing the products of the components of the inertia tensor, $I_{ij}$, and the corresponding components of the angular velocity vector, $\omega_j$. The inertia tensor, $I_{ij}$, is a second-order tensor that describes how an object's mass is distributed in relation to the coordinate axes and thus its resistance to angular acceleration. The angular velocity vector, $\omega_j$, describes the rate and axis of rotation of the rigid body. The summation is performed over the index $j$ from 1 to 3, implying that each component of the angular momentum is a linear combination of all components of the angular velocity, weighted by the appropriate components of the inertia tensor.
angular-momentum-component.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the definition of angular momentum for a system of particles and its generalization to a continuous rigid body. It is derived by considering the linear momentum of each mass element within the body and its position relative to the axis of rotation. In its tensor form, it elegantly expresses the relationship between the angular momentum and angular velocity vectors, which is fundamental in rotational dynamics and is directly related to the rotational symmetry of physical laws.
angular-momentum-component.limits_and_boundary: If the angular velocity is zero (i.e., $\omega_j = 0$ for all $j$), then the angular momentum component $L_i$ will also be zero, as expected for a non-rotating body. If the body is rotating very rapidly, the angular momentum components will be large, proportional to the angular velocity. In the limit of a point mass or a body with highly symmetric mass distribution (e.g., a sphere), the inertia tensor may simplify, leading to a more direct proportionality between $L_i$ and $\omega_i$ along principal axes.

L_i.name: Angular Momentum Component
L_i.description: The $i$-th component of the angular momentum vector of the rigid body. For example, $L_1$ would be the component along the x-axis.

I_{ij}.name: Inertia Tensor Component
I_{ij}.description: The component of the inertia tensor of the rigid body, representing how mass is distributed relative to the $i$-th and $j$-th axes. $i$ and $j$ refer to the spatial coordinate axes (e.g., 1 for x, 2 for y, 3 for z).

\\omega_j.name: Angular Velocity Component
\\omega_j.description: The $j$-th component of the angular velocity vector of the rigid body. It describes the rate of rotation about the $j$-th axis.

planck-length.title: Planck Length
planck-length.conceptual_definition: The Planck length, denoted $\ell_P$ or $L_{\text{Planck}}$, is the length scale at which the quantum uncertainty in position for a particle, as described by its Compton wavelength, becomes comparable to its Schwarzschild radius. It is defined by the equation $\ell_P = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar G}{c^3}}$, combining the reduced Planck constant $\hbar$, the gravitational constant $G$, and the speed of light $c$.
planck-length.intuitive_summary: The Planck length can be thought of as the 'pixel size' of spacetime. It is the shortest possible distance that has any physical meaning; measuring anything smaller is believed to be impossible due to the extreme quantum gravitational effects that would arise, such as the creation of microscopic black holes.
planck-length.interpretation: The Planck length, $\ell_P$, is derived from three fundamental physical constants: the speed of light in vacuum, $c$, which defines the structure of spacetime in relativity; the reduced Planck constant, $\hbar$, which quantifies the scale of quantum mechanics; and the gravitational constant, $G$, which sets the strength of gravity. The defining formula is $\ell_P = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar G}{c^3}}$. This combination of constants from relativity, quantum mechanics, and gravity yields a length scale of approximately $1.616 \times 10^{-35}$ meters. It is widely theorized to be the minimum meaningful length, the scale at which quantum gravitational effects dominate and the classical description of a smooth spacetime manifold breaks down. Theories like string theory and loop quantum gravity operate at or near this fundamental scale.
planck-length.symmetry_origin: The Planck length is not derived from a specific symmetry via Noether's theorem. Instead, it is constructed through dimensional analysis from fundamental constants ($c$, $G$, $\hbar$) that are themselves cornerstones of theories with profound symmetries (Lorentz invariance for $c$, diffeomorphism invariance for $G$). The Planck scale itself represents a regime where the symmetries of General Relativity and the Standard Model are expected to merge into a more fundamental, unified symmetry of quantum gravity.
planck-length.limits_and_boundary: The Planck length $\ell_P$ is a constant value. However, its conceptual significance can be understood by considering its behavior in various theoretical limits. In the classical limit where the reduced Planck constant $\hbar \to 0$, the Planck length $\ell_P \to 0$, recovering a smooth, continuous spacetime. Similarly, in a non-gravitational universe where the gravitational constant $G \to 0$, we find $\ell_P \to 0$. This demonstrates that the Planck length is a fundamentally quantum and gravitational scale. In the non-relativistic limit where the speed of light $c \to \infty$, the Planck length also vanishes, $\ell_P \to 0$, highlighting its relativistic nature.

L_{\\text{Planck}}.name: Planck Length
L_{\\text{Planck}}.description: The fundamental unit of length in the system of Planck units, representing the scale where quantum gravity effects become significant. Also denoted $\ell_P$.
